files.lesson.md: --- order: 17 unit: lines9 node: AC9M9A03 n5 uses: [AC9M9A03 n1, AC9M9A03 n2, AC9M9A03 n3, AC9M9A03 n4] assumes: [AC9M9A03 n1, AC9M9A03 n2, AC9M9A03 n3, AC9M9A03 n4] connection: crow-flies title: Gradient, distance and midpoint together summary: "A real plan can need all three: is a point on a path, how long is the path, and where is its middle? Then judge whether a straight-line answer fits the real walk." language: maths voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 } hook: "A park plan has a gate, a pond and a straight path between them. Is the bench on the path, how long is it, and where should the bin go?" app: command: node "$REPO_ROOT/tools/serve.mjs" "$REPO_ROOT/dist/_playground-board" 8364 url: http://127.0.0.1:8364/index.html readySelector: "#board" layout: full --- You now have three tools for two points: the gradient, the distance and the midpoint. Real problems ask for them together. ## Predict: on the path? ```step stage: predict insight: "Committing on whether a bench sits on a straight path shows who trusts the look of the plan and who compares gradients." check: type: predict q: "On a park plan in metres, a straight path runs from the gate G (2, 1) to the pond P (6, 9). A bench is at (3, 3). Is the bench on the path?" options: - "Yes, it's on the path" - "No, it's to the left of the path" - "No, it's to the right of the path" - "You can't tell without measuring" actual: "Yes. The path goes up 8 for 4 across: gradient 2. From the gate to the bench is 2 up for 1 across: also gradient 2. Same gradient from the same point, so the bench is on the path." ``` The bench looks close. Is it exactly on the path? ## Run: find the points on the path ```step stage: run insight: "Dragging a point and watching its gradient from the gate shows that points on the path all have the same gradient as the path." try: { playground: board, starter: "plan.yml#run", height: 560 } check: { type: board, text: "Drag $T$ to any point on the path, away from the gate. What do you notice about the dashed sides? Was your prediction right?", when: "v = 2 * h and h > 0" } ``` Drag $T$ along the path. The dashed triangle starts at the gate $G$. ## Investigate: three tools, one plan ```step stage: investigate insight: "The gradient says whether a point is on the path, the distance says how long it is, and the midpoint says where its middle is. Each answer only fits the straight line." tasks: - check: type: number q: "What is the gradient of the path from $G(2, 1)$ to $P(6, 9)$?" answer: 2 explain: "Rise 9 − 1 = 8, run 6 − 2 = 4. 8 ÷ 4 = 2." smaller: check: { type: "number", q: "How far up does the path go from $G(2, 1)$ to $P(6, 9)$?", answer: 8, explain: "9 − 1 = 8." } - check: type: number q: "How long is the straight path from $G(2, 1)$ to $P(6, 9)$, in metres to 1 decimal place?" answer: 8.9 tolerance: 0.05 explain: "Across 4, up 8: 16 + 64 = 80. √80 ≈ 8.9 m." - check: type: question q: "A bin goes halfway along the path. Where is it?" options: ["$(4, 5)$", "$(8, 10)$", "$(4, 8)$", "$(2, 4)$"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "That adds without halving.", "Halve the y-coordinates too: (1 + 9) ÷ 2 = 5.", "That's the step from G to P, halved: add it to G."] explain: "(2 + 6) ÷ 2 = 4 and (1 + 9) ÷ 2 = 5." - check: type: bug code: "working.txt#mia" text: "Mia checks whether a post at $(5, 6)$ is on the path from $G(2, 1)$. Click the line where her working goes wrong." answer: 3 fault: logic misconception: gradient-coordinates-not-differences explain: "Line 3: she divided the post's own coordinates, 6 ÷ 5. The gradient from G uses the differences: (6 − 1) ÷ (5 − 2) = 5/3, which isn't 2, so the post is not on the path." ``` ### Is it on the path? Here's checking a point against a line, using the gradient. ```worked A(1, 2),\; B(7, 10),\; T(4, 6) :: Is T on the line from A to B? m_{AB} = \frac{10 - 2}{7 - 1} = \frac{8}{6} = \frac{4}{3} :: The gradient of the whole line. m_{AT} = \frac{6 - 2}{4 - 1} = \frac{4}{3} :: The gradient from A to T. \frac{4}{3} = \frac{4}{3} :: Same gradient from the same point A. \text{T is on the line AB} :: Yes. ``` Now try one on paper: the line from $(0, 1)$ to $(6, 4)$. Find its gradient, then type it. (Then check whether $(4, 3)$ is on it.) ### How long? ### The bin ### Find the mistake Read Mia's working. Which line divides the wrong numbers? ## Modify: place things on the plan ```step stage: modify insight: "Placing a point from a rule, and then asking whether the straight-line answer is the real walking distance." try: { playground: board, starter: "plan.yml#vary", height: 560 } tasks: - hint: ["Average the coordinates of G and P.", "(2 + 6) ÷ 2 and (1 + 9) ÷ 2."] check: { type: board, text: "Drag $M$ to the midpoint of the path.", when: "x(M) = 4 and y(M) = 5" } - hint: ["Gradient 2 means up 2 for each 1 across.", "3 across is how far up?"] check: { type: board, text: "Drag $T$ so it's on the path, 3 across from the gate (and so 6 up).", when: "h = 3 and v = 6" } - hint: ["The straight line is the shortest way between two points.", "A real path that bends is longer."] check: { type: question, q: "The real walkway bends round the pond. Is the straight-line distance GP bigger or smaller than the real walk?", options: ["Smaller: a straight line is the shortest way", "Bigger: it cuts across", "The same: it's a distance either way"], answer: 0, feedback: [null, "A straight line can't be longer than a bent route between the same points.", "A bend makes the walk longer."], explain: "The straight line is the shortest route between two points, so the real walk is at least as long." } ``` ### The midpoint ### On the path ### Real or straight ## Practise: mixed problems ```step stage: practise insight: "Choosing the right tool for each question on a plan: gradient, distance or midpoint." tasks: - check: type: number q: "A path goes from $(1, 2)$ to $(5, 10)$. What is the $y$-coordinate of its midpoint?" answer: 6 explain: "(2 + 10) ÷ 2 = 6." - check: type: number q: "A path goes from $(0, 0)$ to $(6, 8)$. A second path goes at right angles to it. What is the gradient of the second path as a decimal?" answer: -0.75 tolerance: 0.001 explain: "The first gradient is 8/6 = 4/3. Turn it upside down and change the sign: −3/4 = −0.75." smaller: check: { type: "number", q: "What is the gradient of the path from $(0, 0)$ to $(6, 8)$, as a fraction $\\frac{8}{6}$ simplified? Type it as a decimal to 2 places.", answer: 1.33, tolerance: 0.01, explain: "8 ÷ 6 = 1.33…" } - check: type: question q: "Is $(5, 7)$ on the line from $(1, 1)$ to $(9, 13)$?" options: ["Yes: both gradients are 1.5", "No: its gradient from (1, 1) is 2", "No: it's the wrong distance", "You can't tell"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "From (1, 1) to (5, 7): 6 up for 4 across is 1.5, the same as the line.", "Distance isn't what decides it.", "You can: compare the gradients."] explain: "Line: 12 ÷ 8 = 1.5. From (1, 1) to (5, 7): 6 ÷ 4 = 1.5. Same gradient, so yes." - check: type: question q: "Review: which of these is perpendicular to a line of gradient $\\frac{2}{3}$?" options: ["$-\\frac{3}{2}$", "$\\frac{3}{2}$", "$-\\frac{2}{3}$", "$\\frac{2}{3}$"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "That's upside down but the sign hasn't changed.", "That changes the sign but not the fraction.", "That's parallel."] explain: "Upside down and change the sign: −3/2." ``` ### A midpoint ### At right angles ### On the line? ### Review From earlier in the unit: perpendicular gradients. ## Make: the park plan ```step stage: make insight: "Returning to the park plan: check a new point against the path, then judge whether a sprinkler reaches the gate." tasks: - hint: ["Work out the gradient from the gate to the lamp.", "Compare it with the path's gradient."] check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "A lamp is at $(5, 7)$. Is it on the path from $G(2, 1)$ to $P(6, 9)$? Find the gradient from the gate to the lamp, and type it." steps: - ["$m_{GL} = \\frac{7 - 1}{5 - 2}$", "rise and run from the gate to the lamp"] - ["$= \\frac{6}{3} = 2$", "the gradient from the gate to the lamp"] - ["$m_{GP} = 2$", "the path has the same gradient, so the lamp is on it"] answer: "2" answerLabel: "Gradient from the gate to the lamp" tolerance: 0.001 feedback: - ["7/5", "That divides the lamp's own coordinates. Use the differences from the gate."] - ["1.4", "That divides the lamp's own coordinates. Use the differences from the gate."] criteria: - "I used differences from the gate, not the lamp's own coordinates." - "I compared my answer with the path's gradient." - "I said whether the lamp is on the path." explain: "6 ÷ 3 = 2, the same as the path, so the lamp is on the path." - check: type: question q: "A sprinkler at the bin (the midpoint $(4, 5)$) reaches 5 m. Does it reach the gate $G(2, 1)$? (Use the distance between them.)" options: ["Yes: the gate is about 4.5 m away", "No: the gate is about 8.9 m away", "No: the gate is exactly 5 m away", "Yes: it's the same height"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "8.9 m is the whole path. The bin is halfway, so half that.", "Across 2, up 4: 4 + 16 = 20, and √20 ≈ 4.5, not 5.", "Height alone doesn't decide it: use the distance."] explain: "Across 2, up 4: 4 + 16 = 20 and √20 ≈ 4.5 m. That's less than 5 m, so the sprinkler reaches the gate. On the real ground, a hedge or a hill could still be in the way." ``` ### The lamp Back to the park. Work it out on paper first, then type your answer. ### The sprinkler The plan, the lamp and the sprinkler here are made up for the task. **Also used in** - **Planning and surveying.** Plans are drawn on grids so that lengths, middles and slopes can be calculated before building. - **Next unit.** Quadratic relationships: curved graphs, and how to tell them from straight lines. ```teacher summary: Students use gradient, distance and midpoint together on a plan, and judge whether a straight-line answer fits the real situation (AC9M9A03, node 5). time: 45 timing: Predict and Run 8 min · Investigate 14 min · Modify 8 min · Practise and Make 15 min goals: - I can check whether a point is on a line using gradients. - I can choose gradient, distance or midpoint for each question on a plan. - I can say when a straight-line answer is not the real distance. struggle: "Choosing the tool. Ask: is the question about direction (gradient), length (distance) or middle (midpoint)?" before: > Students need the four earlier lessons of this unit. The one idea: the three tools answer different questions about the same two points. The common mistake is dividing a point's own coordinates instead of the differences (Mia's working). The park, the bench, the lamp and the sprinkler are made up for the task. A hedge or a hill could change whether a real sprinkler reaches. running: - "Predict: take a show of hands. Those who chose 'You can't tell' haven't linked gradient to a point being on a line." - "Run: ask students to say the gradient of the dashed triangle each time they place T." - "Paper: the try-one after the worked example and the lamp in Make are worked on paper first. Books out, and look for the differences written before the division." - "Modify: before they drag T, ask how far up 3 across will be." stuck: - see: A student divides a point's own coordinates for the gradient. ask: From which point to which point? fix: "Subtract the gate's coordinates first: rise 5, run 3." - see: A student chooses the wrong tool. ask: Is the question about direction, length or the middle? fix: Direction is gradient, length is distance, middle is midpoint. stretch: Where along the path is the point one third of the way from the gate? support: Print the plan on squared paper and count the rise and run. leads: > Continues AC9M9A03 node 5. Where it leads: Quadratic relationships (next unit), and proofs with coordinates in Year 10. exit: q: A path goes from (0, 0) to (6, 8). How long is it, and where is its midpoint? a: 10, and (3, 4). explain: > The gradient tells you whether a point is on a line, the distance tells you how long it is, and the midpoint tells you where the middle is. A straight-line answer is the shortest possible: a real path that bends is longer. ```

files.working.txt:
# Mia's working for the "find the mistake" task. Plain text: students click the wrong line, nothing runs.

# region: mia
Is the post (5, 6) on the path from G(2, 1) to P(6, 9)?
Gradient of the path: (9 - 1) / (6 - 2) = 8 / 4 = 2
Gradient from G to the post: 6 / 5 = 1.2
1.2 is not 2, so the post is not on the path.
# endregion
